trial_name: EXACT — Lower vs Higher Oxygen Saturation Targets in OHCA (2022)
citation: Bernard SA, Bray JE, Smith K, et al; for the EXACT Investigators. Effect of lower vs higher oxygen saturation targets on survival to hospital discharge among patients resuscitated after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest: the EXACT randomized clinical trial. JAMA. 2022;328(18):1818-1826.
one_liner: In adult OHCA survivors, targeting SpO2 90–94% vs 98–100% from prehospital to ICU did not improve survival to discharge and was associated with more hypoxaemia and rearrest.

pico.population: Adults with OHCA of presumed cardiac cause, sustained ROSC, coma (GCS ≤8), advanced airway, and SpO2 ≥95% at randomisation.
pico.intervention: Oxygen titration to SpO2 90–94% from prehospital randomisation through ED care until first arterial blood gas in ICU.
pico.comparison: Oxygen titration to SpO2 98–100% over same period.

background.existing_knowledge: After ROSC, hyperoxaemia is common and linked to worse outcomes in observational studies, but even brief hypoxaemia may exacerbate secondary brain injury. The optimal early oxygen strategy is uncertain.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether a lower vs higher oxygen saturation target improves survival to discharge.
background.hypothesis: Targeting SpO2 90–94% would improve survival to hospital discharge compared to 98–100%.

methods.design: Multicentre, parallel-group, randomised clinical trial with prehospital randomisation.
methods.setting: Two Australian states (Victoria and South Australia), two EMS systems, 15 receiving hospitals. Enrolment May 2017 – March 2020.

inclusion: Adults (≥18 years) with OHCA of presumed cardiac cause
Advanced airway in situ (ETT or SGA)
SpO2 ≥95% at randomisation while receiving high inspired oxygen
exclusion: Obvious non-cardiac aetiology (respiratory, trauma, hanging, drowning)
Pre-arrest dependence in activities of daily living or known treatment limitations

methods.intervention: Lower oxygen target: SpO2 90–94% from randomisation until first ICU arterial blood gas. 100% oxygen permitted for intubation and hypoxic events.
methods.comparison: Higher oxygen target: SpO2 98–100% over same period.
methods.blinding: Open-label; prehospital and in-hospital clinicians not blinded. Outcome assessment at 12 months was blinded.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 1416; stopped at 428 due to COVID-19 pandemic.
secondary_outcomes: Hypoxaemia requiring 100% oxygen prior to ICU admission
Rearrest requiring CPR prior to ICU admission
Hypoxia with rearrest prior to ICU admission
methods.follow_up: In-hospital to discharge; telephone follow-up at 12 months (80.3% of hospital survivors).

headline_bullets: Primary outcome: survival to discharge 38.3% (lower) vs 47.9% (higher); OR 0.68 (95% CI 0.46–1.00, P=0.05).
Lower-target group had more hypoxaemia <90% (33.6% vs 10.0%) and hypoxaemia with rearrest (8.4% vs 0.5%).
No clear benefit in neurological outcomes or hospital length of stay.

outcomes_table.note: Absolute difference −9.6 percentage points (95% CI −18.9 to −0.2)
Absolute difference 23.7 percentage points (95% CI 15.8 to 31.5)

outcomes_table.outcome: Hypoxia requiring 100% oxygen prior to ICU admission
outcomes_table.note: Absolute difference 20.5 percentage points (95% CI 14.6 to 26.4)

outcomes_table.outcome: Rearrest requiring CPR prior to ICU admission
outcomes_table.note: Absolute difference 6.4 percentage points (95% CI −0.3 to 13.1)

outcomes_table.outcome: Hypoxia with rearrest prior to ICU admission
outcomes_table.note: Absolute difference 7.9 percentage points (95% CI 4.0 to 11.7)
ICU denominator excludes those not admitted to ICU
Discharge destination analysed among survivors only

subgroup_table.note: Subgroup of primary outcome; interaction P=0.01
Subgroup of primary outcome; interpret cautiously given multiplicity

safety: Sustained hypoxic events (SpO2 <90% unresponsive to 100% oxygen): 5 (2.3%) lower vs 3 (1.4%) higher target.
Rearrest with hypoxia (SpO2 <90%): 3 (1.4%) all in lower-target group.

domains.notes: Prehospital randomisation enabled early intervention but introduced operational exclusions (e.g., no randomisation envelope). Baseline characteristics were broadly similar (age median 65 years, male ~77%, bystander CPR ~80% in both groups).
Open-label oxygen targeting may influence co-interventions; however, primary outcome is objective. Neurologic status assessed by CPC, which can be influenced by documentation quality.
428 randomised; 425 included in primary analysis (214 vs 211). Exclusions for consent/withdrawal. Complete in-hospital follow-up; 12-month follow-up incomplete (80.3% of survivors).
Clear oxygen delivery separation in prehospital/ED phase (ED arrival oxygen flow median 2 vs 12 L/min). Lower-target arm had frequent hypoxaemia excursions, indicating difficulty maintaining target.
Groups well balanced on key prognostic factors.

internal_validity.verdict: The randomised design and objective primary outcome support causal inference; however, open-label delivery, early termination, and frequent hypoxaemic excursions in the lower-target arm introduce meaningful uncertainty about whether harm is inherent to oxygen restriction or difficulty maintaining the target.

domains.notes: Applies to adult OHCA with presumed cardiac cause, sustained ROSC, coma, advanced airway, and initial SpO2 ≥95%. Excluded non-cardiac aetiologies, trauma, drowning, etc.

Conducted in two Australian EMS systems with established post-arrest pathways. Implementation elsewhere may be limited by pulse oximetry reliability, oxygen blending capability, transport times, and local targets.

external_validity.verdict: Moderate—highly relevant to similar EMS/hospital systems treating adult cardiac-cause OHCA with early ROSC, but less generalisable to arrests of respiratory aetiology or settings without consistent monitoring and oxygen blending capability.

strengths: Prehospital randomisation captures early intervention window.
Multicentre, pragmatic design across two EMS systems and 15 hospitals.
Objective primary outcome with complete in-hospital follow-up.
Detailed reporting of oxygen delivery and physiological separation.
limitations: Early stopping due to COVID-19 (428/1416 planned) reduced power and increased uncertainty.
Open-label design may influence co-interventions and withdrawal-of-care decisions.
Lower-target arm experienced frequent hypoxaemia, suggesting practical difficulty maintaining the narrow target.
Selected population (already well oxygenated, presumed cardiac cause, advanced airway) may not reflect all post-arrest patients.
Long-term outcomes incomplete (80.3% follow-up) and not powered for inference.

critical_appraisal.summary: EXACT provides moderate-quality evidence that targeting SpO2 90–94% after OHCA may increase harm, primarily due to inadvertent hypoxaemia; early termination and open-label design limit confidence, but the consistent safety signal supports avoidance of aggressive oxygen restriction.

sections.authors_conclusion: Titrate oxygen after ROSC to avoid both hypoxaemia and sustained hyperoxaemia, recognising that overly aggressive early oxygen restriction may be difficult to implement safely in routine care.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: After ROSC in OHCA patients, avoid targeting SpO2 90–94% as a routine strategy; instead, titrate oxygen to prevent hypoxaemia while avoiding sustained hyperoxaemia (e.g., SpO2 94–98%).
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult OHCA patients with presumed cardiac cause, sustained ROSC, coma, advanced airway, and initial SpO2 ≥95%.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: This does not mean that normoxia or slight hyperoxaemia is harmful; rather, the lower target of 90–94% risked excessive hypoxaemia.
implementation_caveats: Ensure reliable pulse oximetry and consider arterial blood gas confirmation.
Use oxygen blending devices to titrate FiO2.
Monitor continuously for hypoxaemia and be prepared to increase FiO2 if SpO2 falls.
Protocols should incorporate safety thresholds and rescue oxygen.

controversies.notes: SpO2 90–94% may represent clinically relevant hypoxaemia, reframing the comparison as 'mild hypoxaemia vs normoxaemia' rather than 'normoxaemia vs hyperoxaemia.'
Median first PaCO2 in the ED was 60 mm Hg in both groups, raising questions about hypoventilation and its interplay with oxygenation and neurological injury.

The BOX oxygenation component found no benefit of lower vs higher PaO2 targets; pre-EXACT meta-analysis suggested uncertainty about conservative oxygen strategies, highlighting the importance of avoiding extremes.

context_related_trials.relation: The BOX trial's oxygenation component compared PaO2 targets in comatose OHCA survivors and found no clear benefit of a lower vs higher oxygenation strategy within normoxaemic ranges, supporting EXACT's conclusion that avoiding extremes is key.

unresolved_questions: What is the optimal safe SpO2 range after OHCA that balances hypoxaemia risk and hyperoxaemia?
Can protocols be developed to reliably maintain a narrow target without frequent hypoxaemia?
Is the harm from lower target due to hypoxaemia itself or to associated co-interventions?
Does the effect differ by bystander CPR status, and if so, why?

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: After OHCA, avoid targeting SpO2 90–94% as it may cause harm through hypoxaemia; titrate oxygen to prevent hypoxaemia while avoiding sustained hyperoxaemia.
